questions.question: What determines trunk encapsulation type on a Cisco switch?
questions.explanation: On a Cisco switch that supports multiple trunk encapsulations, the encapsulation setting selects the trunk format, such as 802.1Q or (on older compatible models) ISL. The platform constrains the choices: some switches support only 802.1Q and do not offer an encapsulation-selection command. The stem should ideally name the switch model.

optionExplanations.A: A MAC address does not select the VLAN trunk encapsulation format.
optionExplanations.B: The native VLAN identifies untagged traffic on an 802.1Q trunk; it does not choose ISL versus 802.1Q.
optionExplanations.C: Port mode determines whether the port is access or trunk, not which encapsulation format is used.
optionExplanations.D: Correct for configurable platforms: the encapsulation setting selects a supported trunk format.

questions.question:
What action is taken by a host on an Ethernet network when the host attempts to
contact a remote host on another network?

options.text: The PDU is sent using the IP and MAC address of the destination host.
The PDU is sent using the IP address and MAC address of the default gateway.

The PDU is sent using the IP address of the destination host and MAC address of
the default gateway.

The PDU is sent using the IP address of the default gateway and the MAC address
of the destination host.

questions.explanation: The IP packet keeps the remote host’s destination IP address. Because the remote host is on another network, the local Ethernet frame is addressed to the default gateway’s MAC address. The router then forwards the IP packet toward the destination.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong because a remote host’s MAC address is not used on the local Ethernet segment.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong because the IP destination remains the remote host, not the gateway.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: destination IP is remote, while the Ethernet destination MAC belongs to the gateway.
optionExplanations.D: The IP and MAC roles are reversed.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the IP header?
questions.explanation: The IP header carries network-layer information such as the fragment offset, time to live, and IPv4 header checksum. optionExplanations.B: Correct: TCP, not IP, carries the window field.
optionExplanations.C: Header checksum is an IPv4 header field.
optionExplanations.D: Time to live is an IPv4 header field.

questions.question: In virtual networking, isolation between tenants is mainly provided by:
questions.explanation: Tenant isolation in virtual networks is commonly implemented with logical network segments. VLANs separate Layer 2 broadcast domains, while overlays such as VXLAN create virtual Layer 2 networks across a Layer 3 fabric and support multi-tenant environments. IP addressing alone does not provide equivalent isolation, and DNS is name resolution rather than a tenant-segmentation mechanism.

questions.question: What will be the subnet mask if 18 bits are reserved for the network addressing?

questions.question:
You have been given the Class C address of 205.222.5.0. What size subnet mask will give you the greatest
possible number of hosts?
questions.explanation: In classful IPv4 addressing, an address beginning with 205 is in Class C (192-223). A standard Class C network allocation uses the first 24 bits for the network ID and provides an 8-bit host field with subnet mask `255.255.255.0`. This yields $2^8 - 2 = 254$ usable host addresses. Using a larger mask (like /16) is not a valid Class C subnet, making Option B the correct choice.

optionExplanations.A: A mask of 255.255.255.255 leaves 0 host bits, providing no usable host pool.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: a default 8-bit host mask (255.255.255.0) provides 254 usable host addresses on a Class C network.
optionExplanations.C: 255.255.0.0 is a Class B mask and cannot be allocated as a single subnet from a Class C network address.
optionExplanations.D: 255.255.0.0 with 8190 hosts is mathematically inconsistent.

questions.question:
Assume you are working on a PC and you are typing www.somesite.in . but you
are not able to connect to it, but when you try 202.141.151.33 you are able to
connect. What might be wrong? (assuming IP address of www.somesite.in is
202.141.151.33)

options.text: The company firewall restricts the access to websites
virus could have caused the problem
The DNS server or DNS settings are not properly configured
The PC is configured to accept only IP address

questions.explanation: If a user can connect to a server by IP address (`202.141.151.33`) but cannot reach it by hostname (`www.somesite.in`), the physical connection, local routing, firewall rules, and target web service are all functioning. optionExplanations.B: A generic virus is an unsupported speculation when a specific networking failure is described.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: the DNS server or client DNS configuration is improperly configured or failing to resolve.
optionExplanations.D: Operating systems do not have an architecture configured to accept only IP addresses.

questions.question: Which statement is true about Layer 3 addresses?

options.text: They are used in routing decisions.
They are only used on local networks.
They are altered each time a packet crosses a router.

questions.explanation: Layer 3 addresses (such as IP addresses) are logical addresses that represent networks and hosts. Routers examine the destination Layer 3 IP address and match it against their routing tables to determine the next hop interface. Unlike Layer 2 MAC addresses, IP addresses are global and are not rewritten at each router hop (except under NAT).

optionExplanations.A: Layer 3 addresses are logical, whereas Layer 2 MAC addresses are physical hardware addresses.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: Layer 3 addresses are used by routers to make routing decisions.
optionExplanations.C: Layer 3 addresses provide inter-network end-to-end addressing, not merely local link addressing.
optionExplanations.D: Layer 3 IP addresses remain intact across router hops, while Layer 2 headers are replaced at each hop.

questions.question: In OSPF, what is the function of a Designated Router (DR)?

options.text: Forward routing updates between routers on a multi-access network
Perform routing only for backbone area

questions.explanation: On multi-access networks (such as Ethernet LANs), if every router formed full adjacencies with every other router, $n(n-1)/2$ adjacencies would be required. OSPF elects a Designated Router (DR) so that routers only form full adjacencies with the DR (and BDR), and the DR forwards routing updates across the multi-access segment.

optionExplanations.B: The Backup Designated Router (BDR) serves as the backup, not the DR itself.
optionExplanations.C: Backbone routing is performed by backbone routers in Area 0, which is distinct from the DR role.
optionExplanations.D: Route aggregation between areas is performed by Area Border Routers (ABRs).

optionExplanations.B: False: inter-VLAN communication strictly requires routing.
optionExplanations.C: True: VLANs can span multiple switches via 802.1Q trunk links.
optionExplanations.D: True: VLAN switching operates primarily at Layer 2.

questions.question: What is the metric used by OSPF to select the best route?
questions.explanation: OSPF evaluates the best path using cumulative cost along the path. By default in Cisco IOS, interface cost is derived from interface bandwidth using the formula $Cost = \frac{Reference\ Bandwidth}{Interface\ Bandwidth}$ (default reference bandwidth is $10^8$ bps). Faster interfaces have lower cost.

optionExplanations.A: Hop count is the metric for RIP, which has a 15-hop limit.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: OSPF uses cost based on bandwidth.
optionExplanations.C: Delay is used in conjunction with bandwidth by EIGRP, not OSPF.
optionExplanations.D: AS path length is an exterior metric used by BGP.

questions.question:
The routing table of the router is shown below:
Destination Subnet Mask Interface
192.168.43.0 255.255.255.0 eth0
192.168.43.0 255.255.255.128 eth1
192.12.17.5 255.255.255.255 eth3
Default eth2
On which interface will the router forward packets addressed to destinations
192.168.43.16 and 192.168.17.10
questions.explanation: In IP routing, the Longest Prefix Match rule selects the route with the most specific (longest) subnet mask matching the destination. For `192.168.43.16`, both `192.168.43.0/24` (eth0) and `192.168.43.0/25` (eth1, range .0-.127) match; because /25 is longer than /24, `eth1` is chosen. For `192.168.17.10`, none of the specific routes match, so the packet falls back to the Default route on `eth2`. Thus the interfaces are `eth1 and eth2` (Option A).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: eth1 handles 192.168.43.16 via /25, and eth2 handles 192.168.17.10 via default route.
optionExplanations.B: eth0 has a shorter prefix (/24) than eth1 (/25) for 192.168.43.16.
optionExplanations.C: eth3 only matches host 192.12.17.5/32.
optionExplanations.D: eth3 is specific to 192.12.17.5, not 192.168.17.10.

questions.question: Which of the following protocols supports route summarization?
questions.explanation: Route summarization (supernetting/prefix aggregation) collapses multiple contiguous subnets into a single advertised route, reducing routing table size and update overhead. RIP (specifically RIPv2 classless routing), EIGRP (manual summary-address and auto-summary), and OSPF (area range and summary-address) all support route summarization, making 'All of the above' correct.

optionExplanations.B: EIGRP supports route summarization, but so do RIP and OSPF.
optionExplanations.C: OSPF supports route summarization at ABRs and ASBRs, but so do RIP and EIGRP.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: all listed routing protocols support route summarization.

questions.question: What distinguishes NAT44 from NAT66?

options.text: NAT44 uses IPv4, NAT66 uses IPv6

optionExplanations.A: Correct: NAT44 translates IPv4 addresses, while NAT66 translates IPv6 addresses.
optionExplanations.B: NAT66 does not provide greater intrinsic cryptographic security than NAT44.
optionExplanations.C: Neither NAT44 nor NAT66 strictly requires DNS to perform IP prefix translation.
optionExplanations.D: NAT66 can be applied across enterprise and internal networks, not solely public servers.

optionExplanations.D: 'start' is not an IOS command for mode transition.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct with regard to Frame Relay?

options.text: Allows the use of variable length packets.
Can be considered as a broadband packet switching technology.

questions.explanation: Unlike ATM (which strictly uses fixed 53-byte cells), Frame Relay handles variable-length packets (typically up to 4096 bytes). Furthermore, unlike older X.25 networks, Frame Relay streamlined packet switching by removing intermediate hop-by-hop error recovery and flow control acknowledgments, delegating those duties to higher-layer protocols (like TCP).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: Frame Relay allows variable-length packets up to several thousand bytes.
optionExplanations.B: Frame Relay minimizes error checking (only basic CRC discarding corrupt frames without retransmission).
optionExplanations.C: Frame Relay does not acknowledge frames hop-by-hop.
optionExplanations.D: Frame Relay is a narrowband/wideband technology (typically 56 kbps to 1.544/2.048 Mbps), not broadband.

questions.question:
Fig 1 denotes a _____ and fig 2 denotes a _____
Fig 1 Fig 2
TCP TCP
IP IP
802.3 PPP
Physical Physical
Layer Layer
questions.explanation: The diagram presents protocol stacks comparing data link protocols under TCP/IP. In Fig 1, IEEE 802.3 represents wired Ethernet, which is the foundational standard for Local Area Networks (LANs). In Fig 2, PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) represents point-to-point leased line/dial-up connections, which are classic Wide Area Network (WAN) technologies. Therefore, Fig 1 denotes a LAN and Fig 2 denotes a WAN.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: Fig 1 (802.3 Ethernet) is a LAN; Fig 2 (PPP) is a WAN.
optionExplanations.B: Inverted: 802.3 is not a WAN protocol, and PPP is not a shared LAN protocol.
optionExplanations.C: PPP is a point-to-point WAN protocol, not a LAN protocol.
optionExplanations.D: 802.3 is a LAN protocol, not a WAN protocol.

questions.question:
Two routers are connected via their serial ports in a lab environment. The routers are configured with
valid IP addresses, but they cannot ping each other. The show interface serial0/0 command shows
that the serial0/0 interface is up but the line protocol is down. What could be the cause of this
problem?

options.text: The no shutdown command has not been applied to the interfaces.
The clock rate command has not been entered on the DCE interface.
The interface timers are not cleared.
The Fast Ethernet interface is emulating a serial interface by assigning it a timing signal.

questions.explanation: The physical serial interface is reported as up, but its line protocol is down. Cisco's troubleshooting guidance lists a missing clock-rate configuration as a possible cause when the router end is DCE. `no shutdown` addresses an administratively-down interface, which is a different status. So B is the supported answer; the conflicting source occurrence that also marked A appears to have over-selected.

optionExplanations.A: A missing `no shutdown` would make the interface administratively down, unlike the stated up status.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: a DCE serial interface may need `clock rate` configured to provide timing.
optionExplanations.C: The source evidence does not identify uncleared timers as the stated cause.
optionExplanations.D: Fast Ethernet is not used to provide serial-link clocking in this scenario.
